source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Eleven LLMs were put in the Wason 2-4-6 rule-discovery loop (propose triple, get yes/no, guess rule). They often test triples that fit their current guess. This slows or blocks discovery. Models with long reasoning traces do better and show less confirmation bias.
numbers: 11 LLMs, task success 6% to 78% within 45 turns. Bias measured as I:C = incompatible tests / compatible tests. Success and I:C correlate positively (significant, stronger for thinking models).
limits: Synthetic hidden rules over integer triples; one narrow paradigm. Correlation, not proof of cause.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that the test step (S4) is where an LLM loop fails: it must be told to pick tests that could break its own hypothesis (S7).

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models (interventions)
finding: Two debiasing prompts taken from human studies, Dual-Goal and Think-in-Opposites (TiO), raised rule discovery on average.
numbers: Average discovery rate 42% to 56%. TiO improved success in all 11 model-inference scenarios; Dual-Goal in 8 of 11. I:C rose in 18 of 22 cases.
limits: Gains are statistically significant only for part of the models; thinking mode gains were not always paired with higher I:C, so some gain is not from more disconfirming tests.
agent_relevance: A one-line prompt rule ('also test something your hypothesis says should fail') is cheap and measurably helps. Candidate for operator text.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models (distillation and Blicket transfer)
finding: Fine-tuning students on TiO-prompted teacher turns lifted success and I:C, and the behaviour carried to a new task (Blicket detector). Prompting TiO directly still beat the transferred model.
numbers: Blicket: Qwen3-32B base 0.57 task success, I:C 0.54; with TiO 0.86, I:C 1.31. Qwen3-8B base 0.32 to 0.40 with TiO. Distilled Qwen3-32B (32B teacher, TiO) with base prompt: 0.77. Wason task: Qwen3-8B base 0.21 (I:C 0.15), Qwen3-32B base 0.41 (I:C 0.14).
limits: Training-based; our agent is scaffold-only. Transfer tested on one extra task. Some distilled-row columns were hard to align in extracted text, so only clear rows are quoted.
agent_relevance: Shows the falsification habit generalises across paradigms, supporting putting it in the scaffold rather than in a task-specific prompt.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models (human baseline as reported)
finding: The paper restates Wason's 1960 human result and Banatt et al.'s earlier LLM result. Humans who tested more disconfirming triples found the rule sooner.
numbers: Humans: N=29; 6/29 right on first announcement, 21/29 eventually right. Mean I:C 1.79 (first-announcement correct) vs 0.24 (incorrect); second-announcement success 0.50 vs 0.19. Earlier LLM benchmark (Banatt 2024, N=50 tasks): best model 26% success.
limits: Secondhand summary of Wason 1960; I did not open the original. Wason's own rule (any increasing triple) is a case where the guess is narrower than the truth.
agent_relevance: Gives the human yardstick for the LLM numbers: LLM I:C of 0.14 to 0.15 is closer to the failing humans than the succeeding ones.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: A Wason-style game over hidden semantic categories (WordNet taxonomy), 12 LLMs, 100 games each. Reasoning models beat instruction-tuned ones, but none is near optimal.
numbers: Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, other instruct models 33-35%. Small reasoning models fail: GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%.
limits: LLM plays both player and oracle; oracle accuracy 85-95% raw, Cohen's kappa from 0.34 to 0.98. Games are built so that the first guess is narrower than the rule.
agent_relevance: Reasoning budget helps hypothesis search, but small models with thinking still fail: do not assume the scaffold can rescue a weak base model.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games (bias vs success)
finding: Share of positive (confirming) tests predicts failure. Oracle mistakes do not explain it.
numbers: Spearman rho = -0.779 (p=0.003) between confirmation bias and success over 12 models. Bayesian mixed logistic, n=1,200 games: bias posterior mean -4.15 (OR 0.016); oracle error -0.12 (OR 0.885, interval spans zero). Bias ratio: reasoning models 24.2% to 39.0%, instruct models 66% to 82%.
limits: Observational across models. Bias measured by turn-level labels; one human annotator checked oracle quality on a sample only.
agent_relevance: Supports a guardrail that counts how many tests were chosen to fail the current hypothesis.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games (when positive tests are enough)
finding: Following Klayman and Ha (1987): a positive test can falsify a guess that is broader than the truth, but only a negative test can reveal that a guess is too narrow. Models mostly guess too narrow here, so negative tests are the useful ones. Failed games drift into hypotheses that are disjoint or partly overlapping with the target.
numbers: Conclusive falsification rate: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5%, GPT-5-Nano 26.6%, Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%. Spearman rho = -0.937 (p<0.001) between bias and conclusive falsification over 12 models. Guess-inside-target held in over 50% of turns for almost all models.
limits: Annotation of hypothesis-target relation was done by GPT-5-Mini, not by humans. Result rests on the game design that makes negative tests the key.
agent_relevance: Test choice should depend on the relation between guess and likely truth; for 'my guess might be too narrow' the test must be outside the guess.

source: Banatt, Cheng, Vaidyanath, Hwu (2024) WILT: A Multi-turn, Memorization-Robust Inductive Logic Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Wason-style boolean-rule discovery with up to 30 test cases. LLMs do badly. Different models are strong at different halves: choosing informative tests, or deducing the rule from tests.
numbers: N=50 tasks per model. Correct: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50 (28%), o1-mini 13/50, o1-preview 12/50, GPT-4o 9/50, Claude 3 Haiku 1/50.
limits: Small sample per model; 2024 models. Rule is a Python lambda over three numbers.
agent_relevance: Splitting generate-tests from infer-rule as separate calls may suit models differently; worth a cheap test.

source: Banatt et al. (2024) WILT (test proposer vs reasoner)
finding: When the tests proposed by one model were handed to others, results changed a lot. o1-mini was very good at deducing from given tests but weaker in the full multi-turn game; o1-preview made fewer guesses and shorter rules.
numbers: Paper reports o1-mini best in the single-turn deduction check and Claude 3.5 Sonnet best in the full test. Avg guesses before final: o1-preview 2, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 3, GPT-4o 4.5.
limits: I read the text and table lines; the cross-model figure itself was not parsed numerically.
agent_relevance: Experiment choice and hypothesis inference are separable skills; a scaffold can route each to the stronger model or add a check.

source: Gandhi, Li, et al. (2025) BoxingGym: Benchmarking Progress in Automated Experimental Design and Model Discovery
finding: Ten environments (psychology, ecology and others) as probabilistic programs. Experiment quality scored by expected information gain (EIG regret); theory quality scored by whether another agent predicts better after reading the explanation. LLM agents struggle on both.
numbers: Larger (32B) beat 7B; instruct Qwen2.5 beat reasoning-tuned OpenThinker. Giving domain prior info did not improve and often hurt after 10 experiments (overconfident assumptions, overfit). In hyperbolic discounting error rose with more observations. Box's Apprentice (agent plus explicit statistical model) did not reliably beat GPT-4o and favoured overly simple forms.
limits: Averages over 5 runs with error bars; small experiment budgets (0 to 10).
agent_relevance: A domain-aware prompt can anchor the hypothesis space. A revise-hypothesis step must be forced after new data.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym (EIG regret)
finding: Good experiment choice and good prediction are related but not the same skill.
numbers: GPT-4o had the lowest EIG regret and strong prediction in several environments; Qwen-32B had higher EIG regret yet good prediction in some.
limits: Few models; EIG is computed under the true generative model.
agent_relevance: Score the test step by information gain, not only by final answer correctness.

source: Joshi, Shethia, Lam (2026) SHELDON: Reasoning through Dual Search over Hypothesis and Observation Spaces
finding: An LLM agent harness built on Klahr and Dunbar's two spaces: it keeps hypotheses and observations as separate stores, and actively looks for observations that current hypotheses cannot explain. Beats coding agents, RLM and evolutionary baselines on four tasks.
numbers: DiagnosisArena 84.00 vs RLM 78.00 and Codex 76.00. ORCA-Bench 66.67 vs best baseline 40.00 (+26.67). ARC-AGI-2 59.17 vs EvoX 47.50 under $2.50 per task. QNN Circuit Topology 1.00.
limits: Preprint, single group; uses GPT-5.6 family models; small task sets. Cost and baseline settings chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Closest published LLM loop that implements the Klahr-Dunbar dual search. Supports splitting S3 (hypotheses) from S4 (experiments/observations) in the schema.

source: Joshi, Shethia, Lam (2026) SHELDON: Reasoning through Dual Search over Hypothesis and Observation Spaces (ablation)
finding: Each of the three ideas matters: comparing hypotheses against each other, a separate observation space, and continued exploration after a first answer.
numbers: Full / w/o comparative analysis / w/o observation space / w/o continued exploration. DiagnosisArena 84.00 / 78.00 / 70.00 / 82.00. ORCA 66.67 / 56.67 / 53.33 / 53.33. ARC-AGI-2 59.17 / 50.00 / 50.00 / 57.70. QNN 1.00 / 0.8833 / 0.8667 / 0.7333.
limits: Ablation on the same small sets; no confidence intervals in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Biggest single loss comes from removing the separate observation space (up to -14 points): keep the evidence store apart from the hypothesis list.

source: Joshi, Shethia, Lam (2026) SHELDON: Reasoning through Dual Search over Hypothesis and Observation Spaces (observation analysis)
finding: Observations that contrast competing hypotheses are rare but carry the decisions. Observations also seed new hypotheses outside the parent line.
numbers: Comparative-analysis observations are 16-17% of all observations but 53% and 43% of verdicts; 93-98% are cited later vs 9-19% for single-candidate analysis. On ARC-AGI-2, 88% of observations judge 2 or more hypotheses. Of 782 hypotheses born after round 1, 204 cite an observation; 158 of those cite one gathered under a different hypothesis.
limits: Counts use explicit citations only (authors call them lower bounds). Some benchmarks are optimisation tasks, not pure discovery.
agent_relevance: Prefer a test that separates two live hypotheses over one that only checks the favourite; log which hypotheses each observation touched.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench: Benchmarking Generalizable Scientific Law Discovery in LLM Agents
finding: 324 tasks over 12 physics domains with counterfactually shifted laws (so memory cannot help). Agents must run experiments on a simulated system. Frontier reasoning models can rediscover laws in simple systems, and fail as systems get complex.
numbers: 11 LLMs. Non-thinking models (GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3) under 10% symbolic accuracy. Overall: GPT-5 75.9%, Gemini-2.5-pro 65.4%. Hardest setting: GPT-5 40.3%, Gemini-2.5-pro 16.7%, all other reasoning models under 6%.
limits: Four runs per setting; simulated physics only.
agent_relevance: Discovery in an interactive system with no recall help is far harder than benchmark scores on famous equations suggest.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench (noise and tools)
finding: Tiny measurement noise sharply cuts law discovery. A code interpreter helps weak models but hurts strong ones because they jump from exploring to fitting.
numbers: Gaussian noise of only 0.0001 reduced accuracy by 12-16% vs noise-free; accuracy fell steadily to noise 0.1 while data fit (RMSLE) stayed stable. Code tool: gain for models with accuracy below 40%, slight loss for models at or above 40%.
limits: The exploration-to-exploitation explanation comes from the authors' case studies, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Matches an Einstellung-like failure: once a good-enough fit exists, the agent stops exploring. A scaffold rule to keep testing alternatives after a fit is found.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: A Virtual Environment for Developing and Evaluating Automated Scientific Discovery Agents
finding: 120 text-world tasks across 8 topics (e.g. proteomics, reactor lab, archaeology), three difficulty levels. Baseline agents (ReAct, Plan+Execute, Hypothesizer) with GPT-4o finish few tasks; humans do much better.
numbers: ReAct completed 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks. Hypothesizer (explicit hypothesis list, CLIN-like) recovered 34% of gold knowledge on easy and 8% on challenge. Humans (16 tasks): 66% completion, 55% knowledge. Unit-test sub-skills: agents roughly 60%+.
limits: Only GPT-4o used; small human sample. Authors' own baselines.
agent_relevance: Agents can do single steps (measure, run instrument) but fail to chain hypothesis, experiment and conclusion; the explicit hypothesis list alone did not rescue them.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models
finding: Generate many abstract hypotheses in words, summarise to a few, turn each into code, check against the examples. Beats direct prompting on ARC; hypothesis generation is the bottleneck.
numbers: 100 ARC tasks, GPT-4: direct 17%, program-only 23%, LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%, human-selected hypotheses 33%, human-written hypotheses 45% (Icecuber DSL search 43%). GPT-4 produced a correct hypothesis for only 49 tasks; 28 of the 30 solved tasks had a correct hypothesis before summarising.
limits: 100-task random subset; GPT-4 (2023). Human selection step is not scaffold-only.
agent_relevance: Propose-many, filter-by-execution is a working S3-S4 pattern; the gap to human-written hypotheses (30 vs 45) shows where search effort should go.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models with Hypothesis Refinement
finding: Propose rules, select, refine with feedback (iterative hypothesis refinement). LLMs are good proposers when a symbolic interpreter checks the rules.
numbers: ACRE task accuracy: direct IO prompting 28.0%; self-refine style (T=3, N=5) 59.0%; raw accuracy 64.0% to 82.5%. MiniSCAN task accuracy for direct prompting 0.0%.
limits: Several table columns were mangled in text extraction, so only unambiguous cells are quoted. Models are GPT-4 class of 2023.
agent_relevance: Verifying proposals with an external executor is what makes the loop work.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling (rule application gap)
finding: Models write plausible rules but cannot reliably apply their own rules to new cases. Their inductive process also differs from humans.
numbers: Replacing the symbolic interpreter with the LM itself dropped task accuracy from over 80% to near zero on MiniSCAN.
quote: task accuracy dropping from more than 80% to almost-zero in MiniSCAN
limits: Tasks are small synthetic induction sets; the interpreter swap isolates rule application.
agent_relevance: Always run the stated rule with a tool or a separate check; do not trust the model to apply its own hypothesis in its head.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SR: Scientific Equation Discovery via Programming with Large Language Models
finding: LLM proposes equation skeletons as programs; an optimiser fits constants; evolutionary memory feeds the best back. Needs far fewer iterations than classic symbolic regression and extrapolates better.
numbers: About 2.5K iterations vs 2M+ for baselines. E. coli growth OOD NMSE about 0.0037 vs above 1 for baselines. Ablations: no iterative refinement NMSE 1.01e-1 in-domain, 1.81e-1 OOD; no skeleton plus optimiser 3.78e-1 / 3.75e-1. Perplexity analysis suggests Feynman equations are memorised.
limits: Four hand-built problems; authors flag recitation risk on famous equations.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis structure from the LLM, numeric fit by a tool, loop on residuals: a template for generate, test, revise.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: A New Benchmark for Scientific Equation Discovery with Large Language Models
finding: 239 problems: 111 Feynman equations rewritten in unfamiliar forms (LSR-Transform) and 128 synthetic problems in chemistry, biology, physics, materials. Best system solves under a third.
numbers: Best symbolic accuracy 31.5% (LSR-Transform) and 28.1% (LSR-Synth). Without data (DataBlind): Llama-3.1-8B 3.61%, GPT-3.5 2.10%, GPT-4o-mini 7.21%. LLM-SR with GPT-4o-mini 31.53%, Llama-3.1-8B 30.63%, GPT-3.5 10.81%. LaSR has Acc0.1 near 50% but symbolic accuracy only 5-13%.
limits: Weak 2024 backbones. Symbolic accuracy judged by an equivalence check.
agent_relevance: Seeing data (feedback from tests) lifts accuracy from single digits to about 30%; fitting well is not the same as finding the right law.

source: Udrescu and Tegmark (2020) AI Feynman: a Physics-Inspired Method for Symbolic Regression
finding: Non-LLM descendant of BACON: recursive search that uses symmetry, separability and compositionality to cut the hypothesis space, plus neural fitting.
numbers: Solved 100/100 Feynman Lectures equations vs 71 for earlier public software. On a harder physics set success rose from 15% to 90%.
limits: Clean noise-free data; the famous equations are now likely in LLM training data.
agent_relevance: Shows that exploiting structure of the hypothesis space (separate the variables, test symmetry) beats blind search.

source: Kramer, Cerrato, Dzeroski, King et al. (2025) Automated Scientific Discovery: From Equation Discovery to Autonomous Discovery Systems
finding: Reviews BACON: discovery treated as problem solving in a production system. It looks at pairs of variables with all else held fixed, builds new terms (ratios, products) until something is constant, and uses a tolerance for noise.
numbers: BACON.1 to BACON.5; derives Kepler's third law D^3/P^2 = k by constructing new terms until the value is nearly constant.
limits: Review text, not the 1987 book. BACON's ceteris-paribus assumption is a known weak point.
agent_relevance: BACON's term-building loop is a compact model of: if two quantities vary together, form their ratio or product and test for constancy.

source: Kramer et al. (2025) Automated Scientific Discovery (robot scientists)
finding: Adam, the first robot scientist, formed hypotheses by abduction from a Prolog knowledge base and planned the next experiment itself. Eve used active learning plus Gaussian process regression.
numbers: Adam found 6 genes encoding orphan yeast enzymes. Eve found that the anti-cancer compound TNP-470 could act against Plasmodium vivax.
limits: Review summary of King group work; originals not re-read.
agent_relevance: Old closed-loop systems already had the cycle hypothesis, experiment choice, result, update; LLM loops add language flexibility, not the cycle.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
finding: A full LLM pipeline from idea to paper, with an LLM reviewer. Cheap but unreliable in the step that reads results.
numbers: Under $15 per paper; automated reviewer roughly matches human balanced accuracy (65% vs 66%). Failure notes: struggles to compare two numbers, ignores a changed metric when comparing to baseline, hallucinates a whole ablation table or hardware details.
limits: Small-scale ML experiments; novelty scores are self-assessed by the LLM and over-estimated.
agent_relevance: Interpretation of results is a weak point; require every claim to point to a logged output.

source: Yang, Du, Li, Zheng, Poria, Cambria (2024) Large Language Models for Automated Open-domain Scientific Hypotheses Discovery (MOOSE)
finding: Builds a dataset of social-science hypotheses and a multi-module LLM pipeline with three feedback loops (novelty, reality, clarity). Reports hypotheses judged novel by GPT-4 and experts. Authors note a trade-off between validity and novelty.
numbers: Evaluated on validness, novelty, helpfulness with GPT-4 and expert raters; exact score tables not extracted.
limits: Skimmed rather than fully read; evaluation partly by LLM judge.
agent_relevance: Feedback loops on novelty can raise novelty at the price of validity, so a generate step needs a separate check step.

source: Jagadish, Rmus, Witte, Mathony, Binz, Schulz (2026) Toward an automated science of the mind
finding: Perspective piece. Four problems for automating cognitive science: representing experiments, generating synthetic behaviour, synthesising models, closing the loop. Proposes an LLM as an experiment sampler instead of a fixed grammar.
numbers: No new measurements. Notes that grammars over MDPs cannot express memory, language or perception paradigms.
limits: Opinion; cites the Centaur foundation model, which others criticise as possibly using shortcuts.
agent_relevance: Frames the experiment space as the thing to search, not only the hypothesis space; no evidence yet on how well LLM samplers do.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) positive test strategy, as set out in Bertolazzi et al. 2026
finding: Seeking confirming cases is not irrational by itself. It works when the guess is broader than the truth and fails when the guess is a strict subset. Wason's original rule is the failing case.
numbers: Set-relation table in FalsifyBench: guess inside target, guess contains target, partial overlap, disjoint, equal; only the first needs negative tests.
limits: Secondhand: original 1987 paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Replace a blunt 'be falsificationist' rule with: ask whether your hypothesis could be too narrow; if yes, test outside it.
